extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in American state government, constitutional law, and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the principal faults of state legislatures and the constitutional/procedural checks (remedies) used to limit or suppress those evils; includes examples of evasions and institutional trade-offs. Useful for assessing the design and performance of state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferiority of legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferiority, as respects knowledge, skill, and sometimes also conscience, of the bulk of the men who fill these bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that many legislators lack the competence or conscience to legislate well; this contributes to poor law-making and creates a need for institutional checks. No numerical scoring guidance; cited as a primary 'blemish' of State government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvidence in matters of finance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes habitual fiscal recklessness by legislatures leading to excessive state and local indebtedness that ought never to have been incurred. Cited as a chief practical result of legislative blemishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heedlessness in passing administrative bills
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to careless enactment of administrative legislation without sufficient scrutiny, contributing to bad public policy and opportunities for misuse of public funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of proper methods for dealing with local and special bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Want of proper methods for dealing with local and special (or 'private') bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that special/local bills destroy harmony and simplicity of law, consume legislative time, and are fertile sources of jobbery and favoritism. Includes examples and citations (e.g., many special Acts of incorporation, municipal exceptions). Discusses that restricting or expunging such bills would benefit governance but that evasions often occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of public opinion adequately to control legislation, particularly local and special bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of public opinion adequately to control legislation, and particularly local and special bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes the insufficiency of public oversight over many legislative acts, especially private/local legislation, which allows speculators and monopolists to exploit public rights. This democratic deficit amplifies other legislative defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the legislature into two houses (bicameralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: First, there is the division of the legislature into two houses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes bicameralism as a remedy: a bill smuggled through one house may be stopped by the other; the tendency of two chambers to disagree is viewed as salutary ('most bills are bad — ergo, kill as many as you can'). Provides reasoning about inter-house scrutiny and examples where the second chamber exposes 'tricks' of the other. No formal scoring but presented as an institutional check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor's veto power (including item veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, there is the veto of the governor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses the prevalence and value of the veto (including item veto on appropriation bills) as a check on improvident legislation. Emphasizes the governor's duty to examine every bill on its merits and the political accountability that makes the veto effective. Notes override by two-thirds vote and risks (e.g., 'Ring' governors using veto for corruption). Includes historical prevalence and constitutional variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the competence of the legislature (constitutional prohibitions on private/local acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirdly, there are limitations imposed on the competence of the legislature, the most numerous relating to special and local (private) bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional prohibitions (e.g., forbidding creation of corporations except by general law) that reduce statutory volume and curb jobbery. Gives specific state examples (Illinois, Iowa, Wisconsin) and documents common evasions: framing an Act as 'general' by applying it to a narrowly defined population, amending general acts to make them effectively private, etc. Notes both benefits and shortcomings of these prohibitions and cites authorities (Hitchcock, Ford).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural safeguards in legislative procedure (quorum, timing, vote thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous safeguards imposed on legislative procedure (e.g., 'three-fifths being present', rules preventing introduction of bills within certain periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes procedural devices meant to prevent last-minute 'smuggling' of bills, the use of quorum and special vote requirements, and other rules. Also explains common evasions (introducing sham bills early to be amended later, grafting new text onto pending bills) with concrete examples (sham bill to incorporate 'city of Siam' used to authorize unrelated local projects). Points out that abundance and minuteness of such safeguards both indicate the persistence of evasions and create complexity in the statute-book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial enforcement and judicial independence (judicial review of state statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of constitutional limitations necessarily rests with the judges, who pronounce whether a statute transgresses constitutional bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the role of state courts in declaring statutes unconstitutional as part of their ordinary duty; contrasts independence of federal judges (life tenure, not appointed by a State) with more vulnerable state judges (term tenure, re-election pressure). Illustrates risks to judicial independence with historical examples (Iowa liquor amendment voided for procedural defect; impeachment attempts and defeats; judges defeated in re-election for unpopular constitutional decisions). Emphasizes that despite risks, courts have 'seldom fail[ed]' to enforce constitutional limitations and are essential to the machinery of State government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting the time during which the legislature may sit (session length and frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting the time during which the legislature may sit (fixed session lengths, cutting pay after prescribed days, and less frequent sessions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents time limits as the fourth major check: most States fix a number of days beyond which the legislature may not sit, or cut pay after that time. Discusses trade-offs: absolute time limits can produce haste and reckless passage of bills; cutting pay vs absolute prohibition; examples of changes (California 1907 abolished 60-day limit in favor of pay cap; Colorado extended session limit and raised per diem). Also covers less frequent (biennial or quadrennial) sessions as an alternative, with supporting testimonials that public interests are not harmed and may be better served, while noting possible downsides (members new in first session may be 'rawer' and more dangerous). Includes statistics (all but six States permitted to meet only once in two years or longer) and commentary on the democratic rationale for limiting legislative meeting frequency.
